rich_text.plain_text: The Skagen painters and the light

text.content: The Skagen painters and the light

rich_text.plain_text: In the 1870s and 80s, painters gathered at Skagen, the fishing village at Denmark's northern tip, because the light there does something the rest of Europe's doesn't. The two names to hold onto are Anna Ancher, who was born in the village and painted its interiors the way the sun actually enters a room, and P.S. Krøyer, whose blue-hour beach scenes are still the most romantic pictures the North has produced. Ancher matters doubly: she wasn't a visitor painting the locals, she was the local, and her small canvases of women working in warm rooms hold up better than most of the grand ones.

rich_text.plain_text: The troll painter

text.content: The troll painter

rich_text.plain_text: Theodor Kittelsen doesn't fit the painter box, which is exactly why he belongs on this list. His pictures for the Norwegian folk tales, the trolls above all, are the images Norwegians still see when they hear the stories. The line between illustration and painting has always been thin in the North, and it still is: it's why so much Nordic work on paper feels like it's telling you something rather than posing for you.
